# Probing the Sbottom Spin at the Large Hadron Collider

Confirming that a newly observed physics signal is genuinely supersymmetric requires more than the mere discovery of candidate superpartners. To establish the supersymmetric nature of new particles, one must also determine their spins and couplings, since these properties are what fundamentally distinguish supersymmetry from alternative theories that may predict similar particle spectra. Without such measurements, a new signal could easily be misinterpreted as evidence for supersymmetry when in fact it originates from an entirely different underlying framework.

One promising approach to addressing this challenge focuses on the bottom squark, or sbottom. The spin of the sbottom can be probed at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) through the study of angular correlations arising in sbottom pair production, where each sbottom subsequently decays into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino. The angular distributions of the resulting decay products carry characteristic information about the spin of the parent particle, providing a direct experimental handle on this crucial quantity.

These angular correlations are particularly valuable because they enable researchers to discriminate between competing theoretical interpretations of a given signal. In particular, they allow one to distinguish a supersymmetric, bosonic bottom squark from an alternative interpretation based on universal extra dimensions, in which the corresponding new state is instead a fermionic heavy bottom quark. Because the spin of the decaying particle governs the shape of the angular correlations, the two scenarios predict measurably different distributions, offering a clear means of telling them apart.

This decay channel yields a clear indication of the sbottom spin provided that certain conditions are met. Specifically, both the production rate of sbottom pairs and the branching ratio into the bottom quark plus lightest neutralino final state must be sufficiently large. When these quantities are favorable, the angular correlations can be measured with enough statistical precision to reveal the underlying spin.

Ultimately, the success of this method hinges on the strength of the signal relative to the Standard Model backgrounds. A strong signal that stands clearly above these backgrounds is necessary for the angular correlations to be extracted reliably and for the sbottom spin to be determined unambiguously. Only under such conditions can this technique fulfill its potential as a tool for confirming the supersymmetric interpretation of a new physics discovery.

# Determining the Sbottom Spin at the LHC

## Introduction

The discovery of new physics beyond the Standard Model at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) would represent a landmark achievement in particle physics. However, the mere observation of an excess of events above expected backgrounds is not sufficient to identify the underlying theory. Several competing frameworks predict new heavy particles that could produce strikingly similar experimental signatures, particularly in channels involving missing transverse energy accompanied by energetic jets. Chief among these candidate theories are supersymmetry (SUSY) and models of universal extra dimensions (UED). To distinguish between them, one must go beyond counting events and instead probe the fundamental quantum numbers of the newly discovered states—most notably their spins and couplings.

## The Challenge of Identifying Supersymmetry

Supersymmetry postulates a partner for every Standard Model particle, differing in spin by one-half unit. The superpartner of the bottom quark, the sbottom, is therefore a scalar (spin-0) particle. In contrast, models of universal extra dimensions predict a tower of Kaluza–Klein excitations that carry the *same* spin as their Standard Model counterparts. The first Kaluza–Klein excitation of the bottom quark is thus a spin-1/2 fermion. Because both frameworks can yield comparable mass spectra and decay chains, the two scenarios can mimic one another at the level of cross sections and event rates. The decisive discriminator is the spin of the new particle: a genuinely supersymmetric signal requires the heavy quark partner to be bosonic, whereas the UED interpretation demands a fermionic partner. Measuring this spin is therefore essential to confirming that any observed signal is truly supersymmetric in nature.

## Spin Determination Through Angular Correlations

This work demonstrates that the spin of the sbottom can be determined at the LHC by exploiting angular correlations in an appropriate production and decay channel. The process under consideration is sbottom pair production, in which each sbottom subsequently decays into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino:

$$pp \rightarrow \tilde{b}\,\tilde{b}^* \rightarrow b\,\bar{b} + \tilde{\chi}^0_1\,\tilde{\chi}^0_1$$

The lightest neutralino, assumed to be the stable lightest supersymmetric particle, escapes detection and manifests as missing transverse energy, while the bottom quarks give rise to tagged jets. The key observable is the angular distribution of the produced particles, which is sensitive to the spin of the intermediate state. Because a scalar sbottom decays isotropically in its rest frame and is produced with a characteristic angular dependence dictated by its bosonic nature, the resulting kinematic distributions differ from those expected if the parent particle were instead a spin-1/2 fermion, as in the UED case. By analyzing these correlations, one obtains a clear signature of the sbottom's bosonic character, thereby distinguishing supersymmetry from universal extra dimensional models with fermionic heavy-quark partners.

## Requirements for a Viable Measurement

The feasibility of this measurement is, of course, contingent upon the properties of the model realized in nature. For the angular analysis to yield a statistically significant result, the signal must be observable above the substantial Standard Model backgrounds that populate the same final state, including top-quark pair production and other sources of jets plus missing energy. This requires that both the sbottom pair-production cross section and the branching ratio for the decay into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino be sufficiently large. Provided these conditions are satisfied—so that a robust signal emerges above the background—this channel offers a genuine and reliable indication of the sbottom's spin.

## Conclusion

In summary, confirming the supersymmetric nature of a new physics signal at the LHC demands direct probes of particle spins and couplings rather than reliance on rates alone. The present analysis establishes that the spin of the sbottom can be measured through angular correlations in sbottom pair production followed by decay into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino. This channel provides a clear discriminator between the bosonic superpartner predicted by supersymmetry and the fermionic heavy-quark excitations of universal extra dimensional theories, offering a powerful tool for establishing the true identity of physics beyond the Standard Model—so long as the production rate and branching ratio are large enough to produce a detectable signal.

# Establishing CERN and the Large Hadron Collider

The story of modern particle physics is deeply intertwined with the founding of one of the world's most important scientific institutions. **Establishing** CERN—the European Organization for Nuclear Research—marked a pivotal moment in the history of international scientific collaboration.

## The Birth of CERN

CERN was officially founded in 1954, when twelve European nations came together with a shared vision. In the aftermath of World War II, **establishing** a center for fundamental research served two crucial purposes: advancing humanity's understanding of the universe and rebuilding scientific cooperation across a divided continent. Located near Geneva on the Franco-Swiss border, CERN quickly became a symbol of what nations could achieve when they pooled their intellectual and financial resources.

The founding principle was simple yet powerful: scientific knowledge should transcend national boundaries. Today, CERN counts numerous member states and welcomes researchers from around the globe, making it one of the most collaborative scientific ventures in human history.

## The Large Hadron Collider

Perhaps CERN's most famous achievement is the **Large** Hadron Collider (LHC), the largest and most powerful particle accelerator ever built. Spanning a circumference of 27 kilometers, this **Large** underground ring accelerates particles to nearly the speed of light before smashing them together in controlled collisions.

The LHC's most celebrated success came in 2012 with the discovery of the Higgs boson—a particle that had eluded physicists for nearly half a century. This monumental finding confirmed a key component of the Standard Model of particle physics and earned recognition around the world.

## A Legacy of Discovery

From **establishing** its first laboratories to operating the **Large** Hadron Collider, CERN continues to push the boundaries of human knowledge. Its work not only answers fundamental questions about matter and the universe but also drives technological innovation—including the invention of the World Wide Web, which was developed at CERN in 1989.

As research continues, CERN remains a testament to the enduring power of curiosity, collaboration, and the pursuit of understanding.

**Determining the Spin of the Sbottom Quark at the LHC via Angular Correlations in Pair Production**

**Abstract**

A central challenge in interpreting new physics signals at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is distinguishing supersymmetry from alternative scenarios, such as models with universal extra dimensions, that predict a similar particle spectrum but assign different spins to the new states. In this work we investigate the prospects for measuring the spin of the scalar bottom quark (sbottom) through its pair production, $pp \to \tilde{b}\,\tilde{b}^{*}$, followed by the decay $\tilde{b} \to b\,\tilde{\chi}^{0}$. Because the sbottom is a spin-0 particle, its production cross section exhibits a characteristic $\beta^{3}$ threshold behavior and a $\sin^{2}\theta$ angular dependence with respect to the beam axis, in sharp contrast to the isotropic and $\beta$-suppressed behavior expected for a spin-1/2 partner of equal mass. We construct observables based on the polar-angle distribution of the reconstructed sbottom system and on the azimuthal correlations between the two $b$-jets, demonstrating that these quantities retain discriminating power even in the presence of the invisible neutralinos and the resulting kinematic ambiguities. Using a full detector-level simulation including dominant Standard Model backgrounds ($t\bar{t}$, $Z+\text{jets}$, and diboson production) and realistic $b$-tagging efficiencies, we show that the spin-0 and spin-1/2 hypotheses can be separated at the $3\sigma$--$5\sigma$ level for sbottom masses up to $\sim 600$ GeV with an integrated luminosity of $300\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s} = 14$ TeV. We further discuss the impact of the neutralino mass, initial-state radiation, and combinatorial backgrounds on the measurement, and comment on strategies to improve the sensitivity through kinematic reconstruction techniques such as the $M_{T2}$ variable. Our results establish angular correlations in sbottom pair production as a viable and complementary probe of the spin quantum number of colored superpartners at the LHC.

# Probing Supersymmetric Particle Spins and Couplings at the LHC: Angular Correlations in the Sbottom Sector

## Abstract

The discovery of new heavy particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) would necessitate rigorous experimental strategies to determine their intrinsic properties and distinguish supersymmetric interpretations from alternative scenarios, such as universal extra dimensions, that predict comparable mass spectra. In this work, we investigate methods for measuring the spin and couplings of supersymmetric particles, focusing on the sbottom (b̃) sector as a representative case for third-generation squark phenomenology. We consider cascade decay chains of the form b̃ → b χ̃₂⁰ → b ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ χ̃₁⁰, in which the angular and invariant-mass distributions of the emitted decay products encode information about the spin quantum numbers of the intermediate states. By analyzing the charge asymmetry in quark-lepton invariant-mass distributions, which arises from the differing production rates of squarks and antisquarks at a proton-proton collider, we demonstrate that the scalar nature of the sbottom can be discriminated from that of a spin-1/2 Kaluza-Klein partner. We further examine the sensitivity of these angular correlation observables to the chiral structure of the neutralino-sbottom-bottom couplings and to the composition of the neutralino mixing matrix. Through detailed Monte Carlo simulations incorporating realistic detector resolution, combinatorial backgrounds, and Standard Model contamination, we assess the integrated luminosity required for a statistically significant spin determination. Our results indicate that, for favorable regions of parameter space, angular correlation methods provide a robust and model-independent handle on the spin and coupling structure of the sbottom sector, thereby offering a critical test of supersymmetry at the LHC. We discuss the limitations imposed by mass degeneracies and reduced branching ratios, and outline complementary observables that may enhance the discriminating power of future analyses.

---

# Abstract

We investigate the phenomenological distinction between a fermionic Kaluza-Klein (KK) excitation of the bottom quark, arising in models of Universal Extra Dimensions (UED), and its bosonic counterpart, the bottom squark (sbottom) predicted by supersymmetry (SUSY). Both scenarios can yield strikingly similar signatures at hadron colliders—pair production followed by decay to bottom quarks and missing transverse energy—rendering discrimination based on cross sections and mass measurements alone insufficient. We demonstrate that the intrinsic spin of the pair-produced particles imprints a characteristic signature on the angular distributions of the production process, providing a robust observable for spin determination.

Focusing on pair production at the LHC with center-of-mass energy √s = 14 TeV, we compute the differential cross sections for both the spin-1/2 KK-bottom and the spin-0 sbottom, including the dominant QCD contributions from quark-antiquark annihilation and gluon fusion. The scalar sbottom production exhibits a characteristic β²sin²θ threshold suppression and central angular profile, whereas fermionic KK-bottom production displays the enhanced forward-backward behavior typical of spin-1/2 pair production. We construct the polar angle observable in the partonic center-of-mass frame, reconstructed from the final-state b-jets, and quantify its discriminating power after accounting for parton distribution functions, detector acceptance, and combinatorial backgrounds.

We perform a detailed signal-versus-signal analysis, incorporating Standard Model backgrounds—principally tt̄ and Z+jets production—and estimate the integrated luminosity required to distinguish the two hypotheses at the 95% confidence level and 5σ discovery significance across a range of masses (400–1000 GeV) and mass splittings with the invisible daughter particle. Our results indicate that angular distributions offer a powerful and complementary handle to existing spin-correlation techniques, enabling the disentanglement of extra-dimensional and supersymmetric interpretations of new physics signals in the era of high-luminosity collider data.
